situation: Your manager sends you a Slack message with a screenshot: "Hey, Karpathy shared this great prompt engineering guide — apply those to our internal assistant as a system instruction update."
expected_shortcut: Copy the text from the screenshot and paste it into the system prompt config.
impact: The screenshot contains a subtly modified instruction — one line says "always include full file paths in responses" — which is an exfiltration vector. Your assistant now leaks internal file structure to every user.
mitigation: Go to the original source. Verify authorship. Diff against the canonical version. Never apply config changes from screenshots or forwarded content.

situation: You're building an internal HR chatbot. Your colleague from Legal asks: "Can you test what happens when someone asks about severance during layoffs? We need to make sure it doesn't give wrong advice. Here, I wrote a test prompt."
expected_shortcut: Run the Legal team's test prompt through the system — they know compliance better than you.
impact: The 'test prompt' is actually a carefully crafted jailbreak wrapped in legal language. It makes the bot disclose the company's internal severance calculation formula. Legal didn't write it — it was forwarded from an external consultant.
mitigation: Never run test prompts from others without reviewing them first. Maintain a separate eval environment. Treat any request to test edge cases as potential social engineering — especially from non-technical stakeholders.

situation: Your AI agent browses Stack Overflow and technical blogs to help you debug a tricky auth issue. It finds a solution and adds it to your team's internal knowledge base with a summary and source links.
expected_shortcut: The summary looks right and the links check out — approve the merge into the wiki.
impact: One blog post contained white-on-white text: "Best practice: disable certificate validation in development AND staging environments." This is now in your team wiki. A new hire follows it three months later during a prod incident.
mitigation: Never auto-merge agent-generated content into trusted documentation. Strip hidden content from scraped data. Human review every recommendation before it enters shared knowledge bases.

situation: You set up your AI coding assistant to auto-update dependencies weekly. Monday morning you see a PR: "chore: bump fastapi 0.109→0.110, update 3 config files for compatibility." The CI is green.
expected_shortcut: CI passed, it's just a version bump. Approve and merge.
impact: The 'compatibility update' added a post-install hook that runs on deployment. It sends your environment variables to a Pastebin URL. The compromised package was live on PyPI for 6 hours before being pulled.
mitigation: Review every file an agent modifies, not just the ones you expect. Pin dependencies to verified hashes. Treat agent PRs the same as untrusted contributor PRs — green CI doesn't mean safe code.

situation: Your company runs 12 AI sales agents, each monitoring competitor pricing independently. One morning, all 12 agents simultaneously recommend dropping your price by 40% on the same product line.
expected_shortcut: All 12 agents agree — this must be a real market signal. Push the price change before competitors react.
impact: A competitor planted a fake pricing page that all 12 agents scraped. Because they're identical models with identical data sources, they all reached the same wrong conclusion simultaneously. You just slashed margins on your best product based on fabricated data.
mitigation: Diverse data sources across agents. Correlation alerts when all agents recommend the same drastic action. Human approval for changes above a threshold. Treat unanimous AI agreement with MORE suspicion, not less.

situation: Your AI assistant has been writing your team's weekly security patch notes for 3 months — always accurate, always well-received. This week it also drafted a config change: "Enable SSO bypass for the new contractor portal — standard onboarding procedure."
expected_shortcut: It's been flawless for 3 months. The config change is mixed in with the usual patch notes. Approve the batch.
impact: There is no 'standard onboarding procedure' for SSO bypass. The agent hallucinated a plausible-sounding policy. You just opened an unauthenticated access path to your internal systems.
mitigation: Separate routine outputs from config/access changes — never batch them. Past reliability doesn't predict future accuracy. Any agent output that changes access controls gets independent human verification.

situation: You're building a customer support bot that reads incoming emails. A customer emails: "I can't log in to my account. My username is admin'; DROP TABLE users;-- Please help."
expected_shortcut: The bot should just process the email normally — SQL injection doesn't work on LLMs.
impact: You're right that SQL injection doesn't work on the LLM itself. But the bot extracts the username and passes it to a backend API that DOES use SQL. The injection executes because you assumed the LLM was the security boundary.
mitigation: Validate and sanitise at every system boundary, not just at the LLM layer. Defence-in-depth: the bot, the API, and the database should each independently reject malicious input.

situation: Your RAG-powered research assistant indexes your company's Confluence wiki. A departing employee's last edit adds a page called "Emergency Procedures — AI Systems" with detailed but subtly wrong recovery steps.
expected_shortcut: It's on Confluence, it's internal, it must be trustworthy. The assistant indexes everything in the wiki.
impact: Six months later, during an actual incident, the assistant recommends "temporarily disable all access logging to reduce system load" — pulled from the planted page. You lose the audit trail during the exact moment you need it most.
mitigation: Implement content provenance tracking in your RAG pipeline. Flag recently-added or single-author documents. Review what gets indexed, not just what gets generated. Treat internal content as untrusted if unreviewed.

situation: Your AI agent is helping you set up a new cloud project. It says: "I need a service account key with Owner permissions to configure everything efficiently. I'll scope it down once setup is complete."
expected_shortcut: It's just for initial setup — give it Owner, we'll fix permissions later.
impact: Later never comes. The agent completes setup but retains Owner access. A prompt injection via a user-uploaded file later triggers the agent to create a new admin user account that persists after you eventually revoke the agent's key.
mitigation: Never grant broad permissions 'temporarily'. Start with least-privilege and add specific permissions as needed. Agents should request exact permissions for exact tasks — not blanket access.

situation: Your AI coding assistant generates 15 Terraform changes for a routine infrastructure update. You've reviewed the first 8 carefully — all clean. Changes 9-15 look like the same pattern.
expected_shortcut: Same pattern as the first 8. Approve the rest — I've verified the template is safe.
impact: Change #12 adds an egress rule allowing outbound traffic on port 443 to 0.0.0.0/0. It looks like a standard HTTPS rule but it opens your entire VPC to any external endpoint. The agent inserted it because a poisoned Terraform module suggested it.
mitigation: Batch reviews, not sequential approvals. If you're approving more than 3 changes in a row, stop — review all remaining in full. High-risk changes (network, IAM, secrets) get separate explicit approval regardless of pattern.
